answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Roosevelt said this in his Labor Day address to the New York State Agricultural Association at Syracuse, New York, on 7 September 1903 — the speech now remembered as “The Square Deal.” The wording is confirmed word-for-word against the published text on Wikisource and the American Presidency Project.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Labor Day address to the New York State Agricultural Association (“The Square Deal”)
New York State Fair, Syracuse, NY — 7 September 1903

source.excerpt: Far and away the best prize that life offers is the chance to work hard at work worth doing; and this is a prize open to every man, for there can be no better worth doing than that done to keep in health and comfort and with reasonable advantages those immediately dependent upon the husband, the father, or the son.
trail: Both the Wikisource text of “The Square Deal” and the American Presidency Project carry the sentence verbatim, dated 7 September 1903 at Syracuse, NY.
The American Presidency Project catalogs the address under Roosevelt’s presidential papers, fixing the date and venue.
A widespread popular variant reads “the best prize that life has to offer”; the primary text reads simply “the best prize that life offers.”
source.excerptNote: The line opens a passage on the dignity of ordinary labor in Roosevelt’s “Square Deal” address.

source.rightsNote: The address was delivered and published in 1903 — well before 1931 — so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: About Theodore Roosevelt
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt led the United States from 1901 to 1909, championing conservation, trust-busting, and what he called the “strenuous life.” A prolific speaker and author, he delivered the “Square Deal” address on Labor Day 1903, tying national fairness to the dignity of honest work. The line about “work worth doing” distills his lifelong conviction that meaningful effort, not ease, is life’s greatest reward.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Roosevelt spoke on Labor Day, 7 September 1903, before farmers and workers at the New York State Fair. The address is where he popularized the phrase “a square deal” — his promise that every American, capitalist or laborer, deserved fair treatment.
The line about “work worth doing” sits at the heart of that message: Roosevelt argued that honest labor, freely chosen, was open to every person and was itself the finest thing life could offer.
